title: What's already happened
goal: Talk about what has happened using the past tense — four ending groups for regular verbs, and a small group that changes its vowel.
bekal: recognize twenty strong verbs that change their vowel
tell the story of a whole day that's gone by
wave: Review **unit 13** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Turn every command into a polite request.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — En lang dag
dialogs.intro: Monday morning. Budi looks like someone who hasn't slept, and Ingrid looks like someone who wants to know why.

lines.text: Hva gjorde du i går? Du ser forferdelig ut.
lines.id: What did you do yesterday? You look awful.

lines.text: Jeg våknet klokka fem. Toget til Bergen gikk klokka seks.

notes: **The Norwegian past tense doesn't change with the subject** — just like the present. *Jeg våknet, du våknet, de våknet*. One form per verb, and that's it.

**Regular verbs fall into four groups** by their ending: *-et*, *-te*, *-de* and *-dde*. What decides the group is the sound at the end of the stem, and the pattern is regular enough to guess. The full table is on the next page.

**Gikk, var, hadde, spurte, sa, fikk, tok, satt, sov, lo** — these ten verbs in the dialogue are all strong, meaning they change the vowel instead of adding an ending. The full list is short and worth learning in one go.
**Hvordan gikk det?** is the standard way to ask how something turned out — an interview, an exam, a first date. The answer is usually *det gikk bra* or *det gikk sånn passe* (so-so).
**Med en gang** means "right away, at once". A fixed phrase; don't take it apart.
**I hvert fall** (pronounced **ee VÆRT fahl**) means "at least, anyway". One of the linking phrases Norwegians use most in conversation.

grammars.title: Four groups of regular verbs
body: The group is decided by what's at the end of the stem — the base form without *å* and without *-e*.

head: Group
Ending
When
Example
rows: å snakke → snakk**et**; å jobbe → jobb**et**; å vente → vent**et**
å spise → spis**te**; å lese → les**te**; å kjøpe → kjøp**te**
stem ends in **v, g** or a diphthong
å leve → lev**de**; å prøve → prøv**de**; å eie → ei**de**
å bo → bo**dde**; å tro → tro**dde**; å bety → bety**dde**

after: Group 1 is the biggest — if you really don't know, guess *-et*. The *-a* form (*snakka*, *jobba*) is just as correct and very common in speech; pick one and stick with it.

Group 2 has a spelling trap: if the stem ends in *-ll*, *-mm*, *-nn*, the double letter is **simplified**. *å kjenne* → *kjen**te***, *å glemme* → *glem**te***, *å fortelle* → *fortal**te*** (the last one is actually strong).
Group 3 is small and mostly made up of verbs ending in *-ve* and *-ge*. If you mistakenly put one in group 2, people still understand.

grammars.title: Strong verbs: the essential twenty
body: Strong verbs change their vowel instead of adding an ending, just like English *sing → sang*. The list below covers almost everything you'll need at A1.
after: Most follow the same vowel pattern as English: *skrive → skrev* like *write → wrote*, *drikke → drakk* like *drink → drank*, *komme → kom* like *come → came*. Since you know English, half this list comes free.
*Å vite* and *å spørre* are actually mixed — they change the vowel **and** add an ending. Just learn the forms.

The past forms of the helping verbs belong on the must-know list too: *kan → kunne*, *vil → ville*, *skal → skulle*, *må → måtte*, *bør → burde*. They're all used to soften requests, as you saw in unit 13.

grammars.title: Word order doesn't change
body: Good news: the V2 rule from unit 3 works exactly the same in the past tense. Only the verb form changes.
after: The past time expressions that most often fill the first slot: *i går* (yesterday), *i forgårs* (the day before yesterday), *i forrige uke* (last week), *for to dager siden* (two days ago), *da jeg var barn* (when I was a child).

⚠️ *Da* and *når* both mean "when", but **for a single event in the past, always use *da***: *da jeg var i Bergen*. *Når* is for repeated or future events: *når jeg er i Bergen*. One of the most common mistakes newcomers make.

blocks.text: Read each row aloud from left to right. The third column is the group — learn the pattern, not each word.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Tell the story of yesterday in ten sentences, all in the past tense. Start five of them with a time expression so you practice the V2 rule too.
Then take ten verbs from unit 7 and give all their past forms. Mark the ones you're unsure of and check the table — the usual mix-up is group 1 versus group 2.
Finally: tell three things about your childhood with *da jeg var barn*. Notice that *da*, not *når*, is right here.

exercises.prompt: Change to the past tense (all strong verbs).

items: The train to Bergen left at six.
When I was a child, I lived in Jakarta.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: Bergen / var / i / jeg / går / i

answers: snakket — spiste — bodde — jobbet — leste — prøvde
var — hadde — gikk — gjorde — tok — fikk
Hva gjorde du i går? — Jeg våknet klokka fem. — Toget til Bergen gikk klokka seks. — De spurte mye. — Jeg svarte på norsk. — Da jeg var barn, bodde jeg i Jakarta.
Hva gjorde du i går? — Jeg våknet klokka fem. — I går var jeg i Bergen. — Jeg svarte på norsk. — Så tok jeg toget hjem.
